title: Born from the dear
hookLine: a father mad with grief; sorrow comes from what is dear; the king and queen argue it through

lines: MY ONLY CHILD, WHERE ARE YOU?
cards: This one is about grief, so go gently. A man's only son has died, a small boy. Since then he can't work.
He can't eat. He goes to the cremation ground every day and cries out: my only child, where are you? Eventually he comes to the Buddha, who sees at once that something is wrong.
Your senses aren't steady, householder. How could they be, he says. My only son is dead.
And what the Buddha says next, the man refuses to accept.

teach.b: So it is, householder, the Buddha says. Sorrow, grief, pain and despair are born from those who are dear. The Pali word is piya, dear, beloved.
The father shakes his head. How could that be? Happiness and joy are born from those who are dear.
And he walks out, unconvinced. He tells some men playing dice nearby, and they agree with him. The talk travels until it reaches the palace.
King Pasenadi hears it and tells Queen Mallikā, and she says: if the Buddha said it, it's so. The king snaps at her: you agree with everything he says, like a pupil with a teacher.
So Mallikā sends a messenger to ask the Buddha directly, and he gives more examples, each as raw as the first: a woman whose mother died, who went out of her mind with grief; a man who lost his wife.
Then Mallikā does something wise. She doesn't argue in general.
She asks the king about his own life. Is our daughter, Princess Vajirī, dear to you? Yes.
If anything happened to her, would sorrow arise? Yes, terrible sorrow. And the people of your kingdoms?
Am I dear to you? Yes, yes. Then by that, she says, you can see what the Buddha meant.
The king rises, turns toward where the Buddha is staying, and pays homage.
The sutta never tells anyone to stop loving.
It names what comes with love: the grief that waits inside it, born from the same person who is dear.

how: Buddhist teachers draw on this sutta when helping people with grief, and many Buddhists reflect on the impermanence of loved ones as part of daily practice, alongside loving-kindness toward them.

o: the grief that comes after a loss

games.q: who said what: tap the pairs.
p: sorrow is born from the dear
no: happiness is born from the dear
is our daughter dear to you?
you agree with everything he says

s: the grieving father accepted the Buddha's words at once
he refused, walked out, and found some dice players who agreed with him.
Queen Mallikā convinced the king by asking about his own loved ones
their daughter Vajirī, the people of his kingdoms, and herself.
the sutta teaches that it's better not to love anyone
it says love and grief come from the same place; it doesn't say don't love.

games.q: you're Queen Mallikā. the king won't accept that sorrow comes from the dear. how do you convince him?
o: ask whether their daughter is dear to him
give up and agree with him
games.why: she asks about Princess Vajirī, about the kingdom, about herself. his own answers show him what the Buddha meant.

practice: Bring to mind someone very dear to you, alive or gone, and let the warmth of them come first.

Then, gently, let in the other side, how it hurts or would hurt to lose them, and let the love and the ache sit side by side, like two hands holding one cup. If it's too much, come back to the breath.

wordCard.voice: Piya. Sorrow and grief are born from those we love. A grieving father, a queen's question, and a king who finally saw it.

orig.note: Pali piya (Sanskrit priya): dear, beloved. the sutta is the Piyajātika: 'born from the dear'.

carryVoice: Your line: the dear bring grief. The love is real, and so is the ache inside it. Take care until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Dhammapada 212–216 (related verses on what is dear)
